records.reason: Hornsey & Imani (2004) is directly retested: the paper tests the classic intergroup sensitivity effect (ISE) and reports the predicted source difference in message motive and threat. No supplied shipped row represents this original paper.
records.omission_quote: Consistent with the classic ISE (e.g., Hornsey & Imani, 2004) participants ascribed less constructive motives to and were more threatened by outgroup criticism than ingroup criticism.
records.identity_quote: Past research has offered two different explanations for this effect (Hornsey & Imani, 2004;Sutton et al., 2006): One focuses on a threatened social identity and the other on the violation of general social norms.

records.reason: Sutton, Elder, and Douglas (2006) is directly retested: the paper tests the bystander ISE and reports less constructive motives and greater threat for between-group than within-group criticism. No supplied shipped row represents this original paper.
records.omission_quote: Consistent with the bystander ISE (e.g., Sutton et al., 2006), participants ascribed less constructive motives to and were more threatened by between-group criticism than within-group criticism.
records.identity_quote: In line with this general norm explanation, Sutton et al. (2006) observed the ISE even among uninvolved bystanders who were members of a third group (bystander ISE).

records.reason: Sutton, Douglas, Elder, and Tarrant (2008) is directly retested: the paper tests the classic and bystander ISE comparisons that the cited work reported. No supplied shipped row represents this original paper.
records.omission_quote: Across three high-powered experiments, Adelman and Verkuyten (2020) compared two classic ISE conditions (i.e., ingroup target: ingroup source vs. outgroup source) with two outgroup target conditions (i.e., outgroup target: ingroup source vs. outgroup source).
records.identity_quote: Sutton et al. (2008) included such a comparison and found consistent evidence for both the classic ISE and the bystander ISE, with both effects being of similar magnitude.

records.reason: Thürmer, McCrea, and McIntyre (2019) is directly retested: the source tests whether the behavioral classic ISE varies with group identification, reporting significance among medium-to-high identifiers but not low identifiers. The supplied row is Thürmer and McCrea (2018), a different original paper (Experiment 3), and does not represent the 2019 finding.
records.omission_quote: In line with previous research (Thürmer et al., 2019), Johnson-Neyman Analyses indicated that the behavioural classic ISE on participants' bonus payment decision was significant for those participants reporting medium-tohigh identification with their group (2.45 and above), but not for those reporting low identification (Figure 1a).
records.identity_quote: Exploring the moderating role of self-reported identification of the receiver, a recent paper (Thürmer et al., 2019) further observed that highly identified group members were more likely to exhibit the ISE both in self-reports and in costly behaviour, even though this effect was only observed in two out of three studies.
